name: Kunu
summary: A creamy, lightly fermented millet drink spiced with ginger and cloves, served chilled in northern Nigeria.
story: Kunu, known in Hausa as kunun zaki, is a traditional non-alcoholic drink from northern Nigeria made from millet or sorghum. It is commonly sold in bottles and enjoyed cold, often with snacks like masa or kilishi.

items.name: sweet potato
items.note: peeled, boiled and mashed, optional for sweetness

steps.title: Soak the millet
steps.text: Wash the millet and soak in plenty of cold water for 6-8 hours or overnight until swollen and soft to the touch. Drain well.

steps.title: Blend the spices
steps.text: Blend the soaked millet with the ginger, cloves and chilli, adding a little water, until you have a thick, slightly gritty paste. A good blender helps here.

steps.title: Make the slurry
steps.text: Scoop out about one third of the paste into a bowl. Pour in 2 cups of boiling water and stir fast until it forms a thick, glossy gruel with no lumps. This cooked portion thickens the drink.

steps.title: Mix and rest
steps.text: Fold the remaining raw paste into the cooked gruel along with the mashed sweet potato, if using. Cover and let it rest for 2-3 hours so the starch softens and it turns slightly tangy.

steps.title: Add water and strain
steps.text: Stir in the cold water until the mixture is pourable like thin custard. Pass through a clean cloth or fine sieve, squeezing out the liquid and leaving the coarse bits behind.

steps.title: Sweeten and chill
steps.text: Add sugar a little at a time and taste. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours and stir before serving over ice.

tips: Use millet that smells fresh and has no musty odour for a clean taste.
Stir the drink before pouring because the starch settles.
It ferments fast in hot weather; keep it cold and drink within 2-3 days.
For a smoother drink strain twice through muslin.

swaps.swap: Sorghum is the other traditional grain; if neither is available, use rolled oats for a milder, creamier drink.
Use a ripe banana or just extra sugar; the sweetness changes but the drink still works.
